Every amino acid in your proteins is one-handed. This year's Chemistry Nobel is about why.
Many molecules have a mirror twin, like your left and right hands. Same atoms, opposite shape.
In a test tube, chemists always got both twins in equal amounts. Life uses only one.
That matters for medicine: in a drug, usually only one mirror image has the effect you want.
In 1986, Henri Kagan found a new way to steer a reaction toward one twin, more than anyone thought possible.
Then Kenso Soai designed a reaction that could favor one twin. In 2003 it worked: only one mirror image formed.
The secret is autocatalysis. The product helps make more of itself, so a tiny edge snowballs.
The Nobel committee noted that, other than life itself, no one had achieved this before.
Now chemists can design drug reactions that pick a hand, and we have a clue how life's handedness began.
